# Cardiac Contractility Modulation Therapy for Heart Failure: A Narrative Review

## Introduction

Heart failure (HF) remains a major global health burden, and despite advances in pharmacological and device therapy, morbidity and mortality remain high. Heart failure is a major health problem worldwide and, despite effective therapies, is expected to grow by almost 50% over the next 15 years, with five-year mortality remaining high at 50%. Cardiac resynchronization therapy (CRT) has transformed care for selected patients, but its benefit is largely confined to those with a wide QRS complex, leaving a large proportion of symptomatic patients without effective device options. Cardiac contractility modulation (CCM) is the application of nonexcitatory electrical signals to the myocardium, during the absolute refractory period of the action potential, to elicit a positive inotropic effect without increasing myocardial oxygen consumption; these effects are independent of QRS duration, so CCM device therapy might benefit symptomatic patients with reduced left ventricular ejection fraction who are not candidates for CRT. [1]

## Mechanism of action

CCM signals differ fundamentally from pacing. This therapy is based on the delivery of high-voltage biphasic electrical signals to the septal wall of the right ventricle during the absolute refractory period of the myocardium. [2] Experimental work first established this principle in isolated and intact hearts. [3] In failing dog hearts, therapy with CCM electrical signals improves left ventricular function and remodeling. [4] Mechanistically, at the cellular level, in patients with heart failure with reduced ejection fraction, cardiac contractility modulation therapy has been shown to restore calcium handling and improve the metabolic status of cardiac myocytes, reverse the heart failure-associated fetal gene program, and reduce the extent of interstitial fibrosis. [2] In human myocardium, CCM electric signals induce reverse molecular remodeling, counteracting the up-regulation of myocardial fetal and stretch response genes and down-regulation of Ca²⁺ cycling genes seen in heart failure. [5] Importantly, a hallmark feature is energetic neutrality: these high-amplitude, biphasic impulses seem to alter intracellular calcium handling, resulting in an increase in myocardial contractility without an associated increase in oxygen consumption. [6] A comprehensive synthesis of these pathways is provided in the mechanistic review by Tschöpe and colleagues. [7]

## Clinical evidence

The first chronic human experience came from a multicentre study by Pappone et al., which demonstrated mid-term safety and efficacy of CCM for systolic HF. [8] The first randomized evaluation, FIX-HF-4, soon followed. This randomized, double-blind, crossover study enrolled 164 subjects with ejection fraction (EF) <35% and NYHA class II or III symptoms who received a CCM pulse generator, with patients crossing between active and sham treatment in two 3-month phases. [9]

The pivotal FIX-HF-5 trial then tested CCM in a larger US population. CCM was tested in 428 NYHA class III or IV, narrow QRS heart failure patients with ejection fraction ≤35% randomized to optimal medical therapy (OMT) plus CCM versus OMT alone. [10] The study met its primary safety end point but did not reach its primary efficacy end point (a responders analysis of ventilatory anaerobic threshold); however, in a prespecified subgroup analysis, significant improvements were observed in patients with EFs ranging from 25% to 45%. [11] This signal was confirmed in the FIX-HF-5C study. A total of 160 patients with NYHA class III or IV symptoms, QRS duration <130 ms, and EF ≥25% and ≤45% were randomized; the difference in peak VO₂ between groups was 0.84 ml O₂/kg/min, satisfying the primary endpoint. [12] The subsequent FIX-HF-5C2 study confirmed equivalent performance of a simplified two-lead Optimizer system. [13] The design rationale underpinning these trials in moderately reduced EF has been detailed separately. [14]

Pooled analyses support consistent functional benefit. A meta-analysis showed that CCM significantly improved peak VO₂, 6-minute walk distance and quality of life. [15] A subsequent comprehensive individual patient data meta-analysis reinforced these findings across functional capacity and HF-related quality of life. [16] Registry and observational data extend these results to longer-term outcomes; Anker et al. reported that CCM improves long-term survival and hospitalizations in heart failure with reduced ejection fraction. [17] Long-term real-world experience with the Optimizer Smart system has likewise been favourable. [18]

## Patient selection, current indications, and expanding populations

CCM occupies a distinct niche among HF device therapies. CCM has been shown to benefit patients with class III systolic heart failure with an ejection fraction of 25%–45% not indicated for biventricular pacing. [19] The Optimizer Smart implantable pulse generator received expedited approval in March 2019 from the U.S. FDA for these indications. [20] Beyond the conventional HFrEF group, CCM is particularly beneficial in patients with baseline EF between 35% and 45%, which includes half the range of patients with mid-range EF. [7] Initial work in atrial fibrillation was historically limited because sinus rhythm was deemed necessary, as the CCM algorithm required sequential sensing of a P wave followed by ventricular depolarizations, and CCM was inhibited in atrial fibrillation [21]; subsequent labelling changes and devices removed this requirement. [22] Exploration in preserved EF has begun: the CCM-HFpEF pilot study suggested improvement in patient health status, though randomized confirmation is awaited. [23]

The technical management of these devices differs substantially from conventional rhythm-management hardware and requires dedicated expertise. [24] Mechanistic and translational insights continue to refine selection, [25] including effects on calcium cycling proteins, [26] sodium-calcium exchanger regulation, [27] reverse remodeling, [28] and patient-selection frameworks integrating multiple clinical dimensions. [29,30]

## Conclusion

CCM is an established, energetically neutral device therapy that improves symptoms, exercise capacity and quality of life in symptomatic HFrEF patients ineligible for CRT, with emerging evidence in mid-range and preserved EF. Adequately powered randomized trials assessing hard outcomes across these expanding populations remain a priority.
